say: Record sales. So why did Maruti earn less? In three months it sold six lakh, ninety six thousand, six hundred and fifty four vehicles, its highest ever for a quarter, by its own account.

A year earlier, it sold five lakh, fifty thousand, eight hundred and seventy four. Sales money went up twenty six percent. But operating profit before depreciation, the company's E B I T D A, fell six percent. And profit after tax fell twenty seven percent.
More vehicles. More sales. Less profit. So where did the extra money go?
That is our question. Did it go into the cost of making each vehicle, or somewhere else?

First, how strong was the demand? The company says it outran supply. At the end of the quarter its network held about seventeen days of vehicles in stock, and about two lakh bookings were pending. And in the release's passage on the domestic passenger vehicle market, it says its domestic share rose two point two points, to forty point eight percent.

So what does it cost to make a vehicle? The investor deck lists every cost as a share of sales. Picture a hundred rupees of sales. A year ago, about seventy five rupees seventy paise went on parts and materials. Now, about seventy nine rupees ninety paise. That is our arithmetic, from the company's percentages.

We rebuilt it from the results statement. Materials used, plus goods bought for resale, adjusted for stock and for vehicles kept for own use, come to about forty thousand, four hundred and twenty nine crore rupees, against thirty thousand, three hundred and ninety five. As a share of sales: seventy nine point eight seven percent, against seventy five point seven three. It matches the deck, which does not define the line. Our arithmetic.

Now the other costs. Staff costs fell half a point of sales. Other expenses fell half a point. That gives back one full point. But materials took four point two. And other operating income slipped a tenth. Add it up, our arithmetic: four point two, minus one, plus a tenth, is three point three. The company's operating E B I T D A margin fell from twelve point seven to nine point four.

Did what it got for each vehicle fall, or did its cost rise? The statement cannot say directly. But we can divide by vehicles. Net sales over every vehicle sold, exports too, come to about seven point two seven lakh rupees, against seven point two nine a year ago. Down point three percent. Our arithmetic, and only an average, with no split for parts.

Material cost per vehicle: about five point eight lakh rupees, against five point five two. Up five point two percent. That is about twenty eight thousand, six hundred rupees more on every vehicle, on average. Our arithmetic.

In crores: had the material share stayed where it was a year ago, that cost would have been about two thousand, one hundred crore rupees lower. Our arithmetic. That is the size of the gap we are chasing.

So what reasons does the company give? Slide seven of its investor deck, on margin movement, lists three negatives. One, quote, adverse commodity prices in the context of West Asia conflict. Two, adverse foreign exchange movement. Three, lower non-operating income from mark-to-market losses on invested surplus.
And three positives. Improved realization. Favourable operating leverage. Cost reduction efforts. Slide seven gives no size for any of the six.

The press release is more direct about operating profit. It says it fell, quote, owing to West-Asia conflict linked commodity increases. That is the company's explanation. It does not say which commodities, or how much.

There is a second hole. Profit before tax fell by about one thousand, one hundred and twenty five crore rupees. Operating profit accounts for about five hundred and seventy eight crore of that. So what explains the other five hundred and forty seven?

The answer sits mostly in other income. In the deck it matches a line called non-operating income, our arithmetic. The release says that income, quote, declined sharply in Q two owing to mark-to-market losses on invested surplus. It was nine hundred and sixty six crore rupees a year ago, and one thousand, eight hundred and seventy four in April to June. This quarter: four hundred and thirty crore.

So about half of the fall in profit before tax, forty nine percent, our arithmetic, sits in other income net of interest costs, not in the operating profit. The filings do not give the rupee size of the mark-to-market loss for the quarter.

But. Here is where our own reading can break. Our average sales per vehicle was flat. Yet the company lists improved realization as a positive. In plain terms, realization is what a company gets for each vehicle. Both can be true, if the mix changed.

And the mix did change. In units, utility vehicles were up fifty two percent. Passenger cars, up thirty two. Exports fell two percent. Sales to other carmakers fell twenty three. A different mix moves an average with no change in price. So our flat average may partly be mix. The filings give no price for any model, so we cannot say how much.

The strongest case against us: the company's list of negatives points outside the company. Commodities, exchange rates, investment losses. And against April to June, materials were lower: seventy nine point nine percent of sales, against eighty point five. Operating E B I T D A rose ten point five percent. Read that way, this quarter says little about Maruti's own edge.
The filings also carry no cost or profit numbers for rivals. If every carmaker paid more for materials, Maruti's fall could be smaller than theirs, or larger. These documents cannot tell us.

One more cost has no number. Note four says the company is, quote, currently unable to reliably estimate a range of possible outcomes, for the rules on scrapping old vehicles. The auditors point to the note too, describing the company's inability to account for it in the books. So the company gives no amount.

So, back to the number. Six lakh, ninety six thousand, six hundred and fifty four vehicles. A record. Materials took four point two more of every hundred rupees. The company lists its reasons. It does not say how big each one was.
The next test is the December quarter. Do materials stay near seventy nine point nine? And does the company put numbers on its list?
